```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_cc <- requireNamespace("CoordinateCleaner", quietly = TRUE)
```

Eight of the tests compare a record with reference data from a shipped layer: points (capitals, country and province centroids, biodiversity institutions, artificial hotspots) and polygons (land, urban areas, countries). The ninth, `range`, needs species range polygons, which the user supplies (see the article on custom gazetteers). This article lists where each layer comes from, how the package's own gazetteers compare with CoordinateCleaner's, how much the choice of land scale changes the `sea` test, and how the reference version is recorded with the flags.

## Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/OccurrenceCleaner")
```

Needs a C++ compiler (Rtools on Windows).

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(OccurrenceCleaner)
```

## The layers

```{r layers}
ri <- reference_info()
knitr::kable(ri[, c("layer", "source", "file", "version", "retrieved")])
```

Each row also holds the download URL, the SHA-256 checksum of the source file and the licence. The tests read these layers:

```{r layer-use, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  test = c("capital", "centroid", "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "aohi", "sea", "urban", "country_mismatch",
           "sea_nonmarine, land_marine"),
  `reference data` = c("CIA World Factbook capital coordinates, Natural Earth populated places: admin-0 capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories",
                       "CIA World Factbook, thematicmapping.org World Borders and GEOLocate country points, Natural Earth admin-0 polygon centroids and label points, admin-1 label points",
                       "GBIF GRSciColl institutions, Wikidata botanical gardens, natural history museums, zoos, aquaria and herbaria, museums of Wikipedia's lists of natural history museums, and BGCI gardens, with coordinates",
                       "one fixed point, 12.58 E, 55.67 N",
                       "Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023), 308 points",
                       "Natural Earth land at 1:110m (default), 1:50m or 1:10m",
                       "Natural Earth urban areas 1:50m",
                       "Natural Earth admin-0 countries 1:50m",
                       "the land of sea, and genus habitats from the Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera"),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

The capitals are the capital "geographic coordinates" of the CIA World Factbook, the source of CoordinateCleaner's capitals, read from the same factbook.json mirror: one point per country profile, 232 in all. The Natural Earth admin-0 capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories (243) are added with `extension` `TRUE`.

The country centroids come from the three sources CoordinateCleaner's table is compiled from, each taken from the source itself: the "Geographic coordinates" of the CIA World Factbook (public domain), read from the factbook.json mirror of the Factbook country profiles on 2026-10-11 (275 points); the label points of the World Borders Dataset 0.3 by Bjorn Sandvik, thematicmapping.org (246 points), under CC BY-SA, from the GeoJSON conversion of the dataset at github.com/jeffaudi/world-borders-geojson; and every point the GEOLocate georeferencing service (geo-locate.org) returns when a country name is entered as country and locality, queried on 2026-10-11 for each country name of the three tables (548 points). GEOLocate also returns places that carry a country's name; one such place, Niger State in Nigeria for "Niger", lies inside another country more than 100 km from the queried one and is left out. The Natural Earth admin-0 polygon centroids, computed on the sphere, and label points (516) are added with `extension` `TRUE`.

All Natural Earth layers are in the public domain; the Natural Earth terms of use say that "No permission is needed to use Natural Earth." The institutions come from the bulk export of GBIF's Global Registry of Scientific Collections (GRSciColl), retrieved on 2026-10-09: 10,002 institutions, of which 6,085 have coordinates. The five of these that the `zero` test would flag are left out: four are registered within 0.14 degrees of (0, 0), although they are in Portugal, Nigeria, Turkey and Taiwan, and one has a longitude of exactly 0. Kept, they would mark every record at (0, 0) as lying at an institution as well. GRSciColl absorbed the Global Registry of Biodiversity Repositories (GRBio) in 2018 and is synchronised weekly with Index Herbariorum. GBIF publishes the registry through its open API and states no separate licence for it.

The institutions are completed from Wikidata, released under CC0, queried on 2026-10-10: every item that is a botanical garden, natural history museum, zoo, public aquarium or herbarium, or of a subclass of one, and has a coordinate location, every museum whose main subject or field of work is a natural-history field (geology, paleontology, zoology, botany and the like), and the museums of Wikipedia's "List of natural history museums", the list CoordinateCleaner's Wikipedia rows come from, and of its Arabic, Dutch, Esperanto, French, German and Portuguese counterparts (2,331 entries, texts under CC BY-SA 4.0, retrieved 2026-10-11) that have Wikidata coordinates of their own: by the article the entry links, or, for an entry without one, by the one museum item of the entry's country whose name it is, when the town the entry names lies within 25 km. After duplicate items are dropped these are 7,810 points (3,263 botanical gardens, 1,835 museums, 2,609 zoos and aquaria, 103 herbaria), none at zero coordinates. The other museums of the lists are placed where the list says they are: at the Wikidata coordinates of the place the entry links, such as the town or the university, if it lies in the entry's country, or at the GeoNames populated place (CC BY 4.0) of the town it names. That gives 700 more points (385 from the English list); entries that name no town are left out. The three places CoordinateCleaner's table takes from GeoNames are taken from the GeoNames country files (CC BY 4.0). The botanic gardens of Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI) come from its GardenSearch map (https://tools.bgci.org/map.php, all countries), retrieved on 2026-10-10: 3,765 gardens, of which 3,653 have coordinates and one lies at zero coordinates, leaving 3,652; they are used under the BGCI terms (https://www.bgci.org/terms-and-conditions/). The `source` column of `reference_points("institution")` says which registry each point comes from.

The genus habitats of `sea_nonmarine` and `land_marine` come from the Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera (IRMNG), Darwin Core archive of 2026-10-06, under CC BY 4.0; cite it as Rees, T. (compiler) (2026). The Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera. Available from https://www.irmng.org at VLIZ. IRMNG sets marine, brackish, freshwater and terrestrial flags per name; the package classes 296,474 genera as not marine and 21,891 as only marine, keyed by kingdom, by the rule in `?reference_habitat`.

The Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (AHOI) of Park, Xie, Thammavong, Tulaiha and Feng ([2023](https://doi.org/10.1111/jbi.14543)) lists the coordinates that recur most often in GBIF records of plants, birds, insects and mammals, with the reason each recurs: 154 plant, 51 bird, 51 insect and 52 mammal points. It is built from the authors' deposit on Dryad ([doi:10.5061/dryad.v41ns1s0p](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.v41ns1s0p)), released under CC0, and keeps 308 points with coordinates. CoordinateCleaner's bundled `aohi` table has 309; the two share 303 points, and the others differ in a few bird points and one plant coordinate (42.26 N there, 42.20 N in the deposit).

The layers are rebuilt from the sources CoordinateCleaner itself draws on, by the scripts in `data-raw/` of the source repository; CoordinateCleaner's code and data are GPL-3, and nothing is copied from them.

## How the gazetteers differ from CoordinateCleaner's

The package gazetteers describe the same places as CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1's `countryref` and `institutions` tables, but they are not the same tables. Measured on 2026-10-09:

```{r compare, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  gazetteer = c("capitals", "country centroids", "province centroids", "institutions"),
  CoordinateCleaner = c("225 (one per ISO3 code)", "660 rows from the CIA World Factbook, thematicmapping.org and GEOLocate",
                        "4,645 (older Natural Earth admin-1 label points)",
                        "9,773 with coordinates (GRBio, Index Herbariorum, GBIF, BGCI, Wikipedia, GeoNames)"),
  OccurrenceCleaner = c("475: 232 Factbook capitals and 243 Natural Earth capitals, alternative capitals and dependent-territory capitals marked as extension",
                        "1,585: 1,069 from the same three sources (275 Factbook, 246 World Borders, 548 GEOLocate) and 516 Natural Earth polygon centroids and label points marked as extension",
                        "4,594 (Natural Earth 5.1.1 admin-1 label points)",
                        "18,245 (6,080 GRSciColl, without the five at zero coordinates, 7,810 Wikidata, 700 Wikipedia, 3,652 BGCI, 3 GeoNames), of which 10,580 from CoordinateCleaner's sources")))
```

- **Capitals.** 221 of CoordinateCleaner's 225 capital points are Factbook points of the package's table rounded to 0.01 degrees, which moves them by up to 523 m. The other four hold values the Factbook has since revised: Bujumbura for Burundi, whose capital it now gives as Gitega; Buenos Aires at 58 40 W, 27 km west of the city, now 58 22 W; Melekeok for Palau, now Ngerulmud; and Rangoon, 1.8 km from its present coordinates. The Natural Earth points add alternative and official capitals that CoordinateCleaner does not hold: Cape Town and Bloemfontein besides Pretoria, Sucre besides La Paz, Naypyidaw besides Yangon, Dodoma besides Dar es Salaam, among others; the test leaves them out when passed the points with `extension` `FALSE`.

- **Country centroids.** 645 of CoordinateCleaner's 660 country centroids are points of the package's table at distance 0. India, Italy and the United Kingdom hold World Borders values that version 0.3 of the dataset changed; three GEOLocate points for Macedonia and one for Guinea, at sea at 10 W 5 N, are not returned by GEOLocate today; eight others lie 5 m to 68 km from a shipped point. The Natural Earth points, which CoordinateCleaner does not hold, lie a median of 30 km from its centroids and catch records georeferenced to the centre of a country's polygon; the test leaves them out when passed the points with `extension` `FALSE`.

- **Province centroids.** CoordinateCleaner's province centroids are Natural Earth admin-1 label points of older releases: 4,566 of its 4,645 rows match a unit of release 3.3.0, 4.0.0 or 4.1.0 by code and coordinates. The package takes the same layer from release 5.1.1, so every province point comes from CoordinateCleaner's source and carries `extension` `FALSE`. 4,591 of CoordinateCleaner's rows are shipped points at distance 0. Of the other 54, 50 lie more than 10 km from any shipped point: 15 hold coordinates of older releases that Natural Earth has since changed, and 39 match no tagged release.

- **Institutions.** CoordinateCleaner takes 712 botanic gardens from Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI), 627 points from Wikipedia and 3 from GeoNames. It geocoded 641 of the BGCI gardens itself from their names and addresses, while the package takes BGCI's own coordinates, for 3,652 gardens, and Wikidata's botanical gardens besides; for 87 % of CoordinateCleaner's BGCI gardens a shipped point lies within 1 km and for 96 % within 5 km, though only 46 % within the 100 m buffer, since the sources mark different spots of a garden's grounds. The Wikipedia rows are rebuilt from the same Wikipedia list with Wikidata coordinates, and the GeoNames rows from GeoNames. CoordinateCleaner geocoded 398 of its Wikipedia rows by hand, to 1 km; the package places the same museums from the list itself, by the museum's Wikidata coordinates or by the town or university the list names. For 92 % of the 345 hand-placed rows with coordinates a shipped point lies within 5 km and for 82 % within 1 km (91 % and 76 % for the points from CoordinateCleaner's own sources). Most of the rest are placed differently by CoordinateCleaner: every Iranian university museum, for example, sits at one point in Isfahan there, and the Museo Marino of Boca del Río, Veracruz, in Venezuela. GRSciColl has also added institutions since CoordinateCleaner's table was compiled. The points from sources CoordinateCleaner's table does not draw on (Wikidata beyond the English list's museums, and the other language editions of the list) carry `extension` `TRUE` in `reference_points("institution")`, so the test can be run on CoordinateCleaner's sources alone. With CoordinateCleaner installed, its table can be added at run time (see the article on custom gazetteers).

The capital difference shows directly in the flags. Records at a few alternative or official capitals, under both references:

```{r capitals, eval = has_cc, message = FALSE}
x <- data.frame(city = c("Pretoria", "Cape Town", "La Paz", "Sucre", "Yangon", "Naypyidaw"),
                species = "a",
                decimalLongitude = c(28.19, 18.42, -68.15, -65.26, 96.16, 96.13),
                decimalLatitude = c(-25.75, -33.92, -16.50, -19.04, 16.80, 19.75))
data.frame(city = x$city,
           natural_earth = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital,
           CoordinateCleaner = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital)
```

Cape Town, Sucre and Naypyidaw are flagged only through the Natural Earth extension points; Pretoria, La Paz and Yangon under both. Which list is right depends on what an error looks like: a herbarium sheet in Cape Town georeferenced to the city is as wrong under either reference, and only the extension points catch it.

## Land scale and the `sea` test

The `sea` test flags records outside the land polygons. The coarse 1:110m layer, the default of CoordinateCleaner's `cc_sea()` (its `clean_coordinates()` uses 1:50m), smooths the coast and drops small islands; the 1:50m layer follows the coast more closely. A grid of points over Denmark and the western Baltic shows where the two disagree:

```{r land-grid}
g <- expand.grid(decimalLongitude = seq(7.5, 15.5, by = 0.05),
                 decimalLatitude = seq(54, 58, by = 0.05))
g$species <- "a"
s110 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea")$flag_sea
s50 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea", land_scale = 50)$flag_sea
g$verdict <- ifelse(s110 & s50, "sea at both", ifelse(!s110 & !s50, "land at both",
                    ifelse(s110, "sea at 1:110m only", "sea at 1:50m only")))
table(g$verdict)
```

```{r land-map, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 5}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(g, aes(decimalLongitude, decimalLatitude, fill = verdict)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`land at both` = "#C8B88A", `sea at both` = "#A9C7E0",
                               `sea at 1:110m only` = "#C0392B", `sea at 1:50m only` = "#2C3E50")) +
  coord_quickmap(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "longitude", y = "latitude", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA))
```

```{r land-share, include = FALSE}
dis <- mean(s110 != s50)
```

On this grid the two scales disagree for `r round(100 * dis, 1)` % of the points, all of them along the coast. At 1:110m Funen, Lolland, Falster, Rügen and Bornholm are missing, so records on them are flagged as at sea (red); the coarse 1:110m coastline also reaches out into the water, so records in a strip of coastal water count as on land there and are flagged only at 1:50m (dark). For coastal and island taxa the scale therefore changes a share of the `sea` flags large enough to see in a tally. The 1:10m layer is the most detailed of the three and is downloaded on first use:

```{r land-10, eval = FALSE}
download_reference("land_10")
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "sea", land_scale = 10)
```

The download is checked against the SHA-256 in `reference_info()` and refused if Natural Earth has published a different file under the same name. The converted layer is stored in `tools::R_user_dir("OccurrenceCleaner", "cache")`, so it is downloaded once per machine.

## Buffers

The buffers are the other half of every proximity test. They default to CoordinateCleaner's (10 km for capitals, 1 km for centroids and the GBIF headquarters, 100 m for institutions, 0.5 degrees around (0, 0)) and are changed per test:

```{r buffers}
x <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = c(16.37, 16.45), decimalLatitude = c(48.21, 48.21))
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", buffers = list(capital = 2000))$flag_capital
```

A buffer of 2 km for capitals keeps records from the outer districts of a capital while still removing those placed at the city's coordinates. The 0.5-degree zero buffer is in degrees, the others in metres.

## Recording the reference

Every flagged data frame carries the reference that produced it, with the version of each layer:

```{r stamp}
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("capital", "sea"), land_scale = 50)
attr(f, "occ_reference")
attr(f, "occ_layout_version")
```

`reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` stamps the installed CoordinateCleaner version instead. For streamed input the same label is written to the output directory, and a rerun into that directory with a different reference, land scale, set of tests or layout stops with an error, so one output directory never mixes flags from two references.

## Choosing a reference

- `reference = "natural_earth"` (the default) needs no other package, has a version and checksum for every layer, and uses current Natural Earth, GRSciColl, Wikidata, Wikipedia, GeoNames and BGCI data.

- `reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` gives CoordinateCleaner's flags up to the differences listed in the article Coming from CoordinateCleaner, for example to compare with a published analysis that used it. It needs CoordinateCleaner installed, and rnaturalearth for the polygon tests, which downloads the Natural Earth layers at run time as CoordinateCleaner does.

Both references use the same buffers and the same geodesic distance, so the difference between them is in the points and polygons only.
